paragraphs: The law declares the general will, and in the same way the censorship declares the public judgment. Public opinion is the kind of law that the censor administers, and like the prince, he applies it only to particular cases.
The censorial tribunal does not rule on the people’s opinion. It only declares it, and as soon as the two part ways, its decisions are null and void.

It is useless to distinguish the morals of a nation from the things it esteems; both depend on the same principle and cannot be told apart. There is no people on earth whose choice of pleasures is decided by nature rather than opinion. Set men’s opinions right, and their morals will purify themselves. Men always love what is good, or what they find good; it is in judging what is good that they go wrong. So it is this judgment that must be regulated. Whoever judges of morals judges of honor, and whoever judges of honor finds his law in opinion.

A people’s opinions spring from its constitution. The law does not regulate morals, but it is legislation that gives birth to them. When legislation weakens, morals decay. In that situation, though, the censors’ judgment will not achieve what the force of the laws could not.

It follows that the censorship may be useful for preserving morals, but can never be useful for restoring them. Set up censors while the laws are vigorous; once the laws have lost their vigor, all hope is gone, for no legitimate power can keep its force when the laws have lost theirs.

The censorship preserves morals by keeping opinion from growing corrupt, by keeping it sound through wise applications, and sometimes even by settling it while it is still undecided. In the kingdom of France, the use of seconds in duels had gone to wild extremes. A few words in a royal edict ended it: “As for those who are cowards enough to call upon seconds.” This judgment got ahead of the public’s own and settled the matter at once. But when edicts from the same source tried to declare dueling itself an act of cowardice, which it is, the public paid no attention. Common opinion does not see it that way, and on this point the public’s mind was already made up.

I have said elsewhere[1] that public opinion is not subject to any constraint, so the tribunal set up to represent it should show no trace of constraint. One cannot admire too much the skill with which the Romans, and even more the Lacedaemonians, used this resource, which we moderns have lost entirely.

In the Spartan Council, a man of bad morals once made a good proposal. The Ephors set it aside and had a virtuous citizen put forward the same one. What an honor for the one man, and what a disgrace for the other, with neither praised nor blamed! Some drunkards from Samos[2] fouled the tribunal of the Ephors. The next day a public edict allowed Samians to be filthy. No actual punishment could have stung as much as that impunity. When Sparta has ruled on what is right and what is not, Greece does not appeal.
